title: What makes a film “high art” for you?

commenti.body: [removed]

I think barriers and quantifies have been broken down enough that enough low and high art, is mostly a matter of personal praise in that it’s pretty difficult to fail entirely at the artistic craft necessary to even make a film, most films are at the very least low art, and some mixture of having something profound to say, that way of phrasing it, the craft of the film making and how a viewer reacts to it defines whether they consider it high art or not. It is a very subjective term.


Outside if that, but definitely related is the equally relegated distinction of the fine arts world between art and *A*rt, where the capitalization usually conveys a larger sense of magnitude and scale, of objectivity. An extreme example of capital-A art would be something like  the works of Christi and Jean-Claude, architects, or medium/genre defining art. Or again, it’s a matter of complimenting something.

I don't think there's a fine line between art and entertainment. To my way of thinking, they are both, first and foremost, an ***aesthetic*** experience.

In terms of defining art, I fall back on the institutional definition: art is what the art world defines as art, puts in museums and galleries, writes monographs about.

For me, it’s often a director and a reputation. A high regard and buzz. But it’s also seeing a new concept. Something that makes you think. Sort of like when you go to a museum and see a piece that makes you stop and think about what the artist is saying. High art in film is complex, it makes you wonder. Rashomon, Mulholland Drive… you have to stay with it every second, but you want to stay with it every second. Kill Bill volume I is high art because it’s visually stunning, and it’s iconic, the acting is excellent, and it’s a tribute to Lady Snowblood. I consider Lawrence of Arabia lower tier high art because yes it’s beautiful, the music is amazing, but the story falls flat.

[removed]
You don’t think there’s an objective technical difference between something like Ant-Man: Quantumania versus Melancholia?

There are quantifiable techniques and some are harder to pull off than others. I think anything that’s going for and achieving those higher-level narrative and visual techniques crosses into art, as opposed to simply being “entertainment” for lack of a better distinction.

And even then, it’s crossing a minimum threshold. There’s still a whole range. Like Scream is art. But it’s not employing all the techniques that something like There Will Be Blood is. 

Great entertainment is just as important as great art. So it’s not like one is inherently better. But when a work can do both—that’s the best.

I think high art leaves room for the audience to complete the meaning of the piece.

High art can have a different dialogue with each spectator based on its ambiguous morals or unique aesthetics.

I don't know if that definition would hold up under scrutiny, but I think "low art" or "entertainment" provides more or less the same experience to each spectator and again on rewatches.

During Captain Marvel, I wondered how much the Department of Defence funded the movie. I thought about the increasing ties between the US military and Hollywood since the Vietnam War. But I wouldn't call it high art. 


In all seriousness, would you consider films with a heavy propaganda element high or low art? Or is it irrelevant?

I did hear one distinction attributed to Andrei Tarkovsky that movies that fit within genres are commercial movies meant for mass consumption. The appeal lf this point is that it often is based on simpler and established rrlstionships of visuals and cinematic editing/shots to convey clear meanings.

Where of course something like Tarkovsky’s Stalker leaves things more ambiguous and invite the audience’s interpretation.

This then emphasizes complexity of a work based on how a movie pushes cinema beyond established norms.

But whether that is a meaningful distinction isn’t self evident to me as I could imagine it being unintuitive by example.

Marcel Duchamp answered this question over a hundred years ago, "Anything is art if the artist says it is."

For context, at the time art was defined and controlled by academies and guilds. To be stamped an artist conferred a certain formal status. Those days are mostly over. Anyone can call themselves an artist and their creations will be labeled as art. 

The question of whether something is or isn't art or high art is an anachronism. The more important question is whether it's good or not.

Its real simple. For me: if it gets under my skin and stays there, then its about the purest form of art there is. 

Films that come to mind:

Angels of desire

Taste of Cherry

Angels of Desire changed the way I thought about living in a body.

Taste of Cherry was literally a disincentive to me killing myself on many occasions. 

Film has the power to change us, just like any other art form I guess. There are a lot more films I could mention that have done this for me. These were just the first two that came to mind.

art isn't defined by any institution nor located solely in museums. That's a very limiting and proverbial way of looking at it. Art is more like the common point in which expression and aesthetics meet. Determining it's value is a different conversation, though

One possible complication to this idea is that, in quite a few cases, works and genres originally meant for mass consumption have, in retrospective climbed the ladder from lowbrow to highbrow.

In the late 18th century, the novel itself was considered a lowbrow format, only suitable for women, whereas poetry and essays and printed sermons were worthwhile reading for intelligent men. The reception of Dickens' novels has evolved from 'sentimental serialized potboilers' to classics of English literature. Mozart's operas and jazz have climbed the same ladder. Hitchcock's reputation, due in large part to *Cahiers du Cinema*, has evolved from 'creator of popular, crowd-pleasing thrillers' to 'one of the great artists of cinema history.'

I guess by that I meant more of a definition of 'high art' or 'fine art.' 

A devil's advocate thought: we accept the institutional definition in quite a few other areas of life. What is science if not "the kinds of activities performed by scientists and scientific institutions?"

Indeed, things of such a significant impact that they stand a test of time and prove their relevance to something more than passing fads but some deep resonance with people.

I do wonder if high art is often just a distinction of taste by demographic. Those who wish to set themselves apart as being elite in some respect rather than different.

Although I would perhaps emphasize aesthetic experiences of some works nourish more deeply than other works. I have enjoyed watching Van Helsing with Hugh Jackman. I think it is very crude and has some tackless jokes but I like the action and the plot is tight enough for me to follow comfortably. It satisfies but not in the way something like The Sunset Limited does.

The distinction I would draw there is a bit like the raw pleasure of something that makes me happy and something that is somehow more deeply satisfying even if in appearance it makes me sad or even uncomfortable. The aesthetic response seems to be more than a kind of fast food visual pleasure. But this distinction requires some theory as to how there can be different planes of aesthetic satisfaction/experience in the way that thoughts and emotions are not crudely one thing but can be multifaceted.

What would offset this would be the deep satisfaction for a seemingly low brow action film or something. I don’t know much about aesthetics to talk of ranking them in depth though. But I do have the intuition of some pleasures being somehow more satisfying, a sense of contentment in the way that one could be deeply depressed with life but still laugh at jokes and experience pleasure temporarily but the overall state of/disposition toward ones life is miserable.
[removed]

High art cuts to the deepest parts of the subconscious mind.

Pieces of high art tend to create extremely unique and specific viewing experiences with each piece. Whereas “low” art or “genre” art tends to replicate very similar experiences each time. 

High art can also contain more complexity of ideas. But I don’t consider this is a necessity. I think its more about the depth of those ideas, and the effort to explore something unique that hasn’t been explored in the same way before.

Ultimately though, low to high art is a spectrum. A lot of films fall somewhere between. 

And low art isn’t inherently worse or less valuable. I’d consider The Matrix to be fairly low art but also a thematically rich, excellently crafted work that is one of the best films ever made.
IMO it’s mostly intent and popular perception. Do people see this as a film that evokes a feeling or as something to pass the time? Did the people making it intend to get that reaction?

Yeah. I think this is best shown with the topic of violence. "High art" shows violence because it's trying to say something about humanity. "Low art" shows violence for the spectacle: explosions, choreography, scale, etc..

I also think these categories can and do overlap. Many timeless classics used to be seen as trashy pulp.

This is exactly why I subscribe to the institutional definition of 'fine arts' or 'high art,' as I mention elsewhere in this thread. Art is what occurs in the art world or, to put it another way, art is what is labeled as art. This avoids a few of the main issues of trying to define what art is: the fact, as mentioned before, that mass entertainment can gain art status over time; the difficulties in distinguishing art from other activities; the fact that we can go to a museum and appreciate a Chinese bowl or a Roman coin (originally created for a very utilitarian purpose) as an artwork. 

>The aesthetic response seems to be more than a kind of fast food visual pleasure. But this distinction requires some theory as to how there can be different planes of aesthetic satisfaction/experience in the way that thoughts and emotions are not crudely one thing but can be multifaceted.

 I'm really not sure you can draw a fine line here. I mean, would you agree that listening to a Mahler symphony and listening to pop song are, in some sense, the same activity? Or at least on a continuum rather than completely separate. 

To me, playing a video game, looking at a painting, watching a blockbuster, watching an arthouse movie -- it's all fundamentally an ***aesthetic*** activity. Any line between art and entertainment is arbitrary and works have a habit of crossing that line.
What objective critreria would you use?

I think the criteria varies depending on the conversation. 

But it’s kind of like the Olympics. They pick a slew of subjective aspects and come up with objective criteria to judge each contestant. 

That depends on people coming to some kind of basic agreement. Which is easier with a smaller group. The more voices, the more debate, of course.

You could pick “character development” as a point and then agree on aspects that qualify as “good”. For instance, is there a change in charge? Does the character go through different emotional states that define a period of the film? Does the film formally react to the emotional charge through editing? Cinematography? Mise-en-scene? 

You could pick something like “average shot length” as a positive. I’m not saying it is. Just that you could use it as a rubric by which to judge a movie’s filmmaking. Others might disagree with that choice. But it is an objective measurement.

>That depends on people coming to some kind of basic agreement. Which is easier with a smaller group. The more voices, the more debate, of course.

Yes, but that's the consensus, not the objective truth of how good a movie is.

>You could pick “character development” as a point and then agree on aspects that qualify as “good”.

Those aspects are still up to whatever standards and biases the viewer holds. And what if someone finds the lack of character developement fitting for the movie?

>You could pick something like “average shot length” as a positive. I’m not saying it is. Just that you could use it as a rubric by which to judge a movie’s filmmaking. Others might disagree with that choice. But it is an objective measurement.

That's an objectively quantifiable fact, yes, just like the fact that *jaws* was released in 1975, was directed by Steven Spielberg and has a runtime of 124 minutes. I'm not denying there are *objective* aspects in films, but the moment you assign some sort of indication of *quality* to thise aspects, you enter subjectivity. 

Just my 0.50.
[removed]

>Yes, but that's the consensus, not the objective truth of how good a movie is.

>Those aspects are still up to whatever standards and biases the viewer holds. And what if someone finds the lack of character developement fitting for the movie?

I feel like those are both things I addressed. Pretty directly.  

I never said this was about the objective truth of how good a movie is. Just floated the idea of objective technical difference between movies, with the subtext being that might have something to do with how people choose to label one movie as art and another as not. 

The reason I made the comparison to the Olympics was because a lot of the scoring has to do with degree of difficulty. And art tends to be craft-based, technique-based. And some things are harder to do than others. For example, there's a higher degree of difficulty in filming a long take than editing together a number of takes and shots. Just like it's harder to hit a home run than a single. Or how a double somersault is harder than a single somersault. Or Tony Hawk doing a 360 on a skateboard is easier than a 720. 

There's a whole other degree of difficulty and technique in editing that has nothing to do with the filming portion. That's another conversation. 

It's the same with writing.

>Physicist Leonardo Vetra smelled burning flesh, and he knew it was his own. He stared up in terror at the dark figure looming over him. "What do you want!"

>"La chiave," the raspy voice replied. "The password."

>"But...I don't—"

>The intruder pressed down again, grinding the white hot object deeper into Vetra's chest. There was the hiss of broiling flesh.


Compare that to:

>See the child. He is pale and thin, he wears a thin and ragged linen shirt. He stokes the scullery fire. Outside lie dark turned fields with rags of snow and darker woods beyond that harbor yet a few last wolves. His folk are known for hewers of wood and drawers of water but in truth his father has been a schoolmaster. He lies in drink, he quotes from poets whose names are now lost. The boy crouches by the fire and watches him."

Very different styles. The first is Dan Brown. The second is Cormac McCarthy. 

Notice in Brown's that there are really four sentences that aren't attached to dialogue. And two of them use the same construction: Noun verb adverb, adverbial clause. 

"Vetra smelled burning flesh, and he knew it was his own. The intruder pressed down again, grinding the white hot object deeper into Vetra's chest." 

Similar cadence. Similar length. Similar build. And he follows both up with single-clause sentences that act as kickers to what was already said.  

The imagery is narrow and vague. You get a range of feeling descriptions——smell, sound, and feel—but the overall picture is thin. 

Compare that to Cormac's. The flow is a lot more elaborate. He mixes in multiple clauses and relies on a wider range of syntax. Prepositions, conjunctions. He chains verbs. There's an immediate difference in the scope of the world. It's grounded in a scene but you get a sense of history as well. There's more musicality. More imagery. 

It's a different level of craftsmanship. And, to be fair, they're written for very different audiences. Maybe Dan Brown could write like Cormac. But that's not who he's writing for. Just like Ant-Man Quantumania had a different audience in mind than Melancholia. 

They're aiming to accomplish different things. But it's an entirely different degree of difficulty and craftsmanship doing what Cormac did. Someone may prefer Brown's writing. Which is completely acceptable.

>I feel like those are both things I addressed. Pretty directly. 

>I never said this was about the objective truth of how good a movie is. Just floated the idea of objective technical difference between movies, with the subtext being that might have something to do with how people choose to label one movie as art and another as not. 

My bad, i think i misunderstood your response.

I agree to an extend that movies are a craft too and that some things take more effort and skill to pull off, and that those who manage to do those things should be held at a great respect for their craftsmanship, but at that point it becomes a different topic altogether from "good versus bad movies", since you could work your ass off making the most ambitious 10 minute long takes in history with the most difficult angles, timing and whatever but still have the movie turn out bad (subjectively, of course) if it doesn't look good visually, the characters aren't interesting or consistent etc.

I'm honestly not very good at articulating my thoughts so pardon me for not giving a longer response, but i mostly agree with your premise of craftsmanship, i just view that as a completely separate discussion from how good/meaningful/effective/whatever the piece of art that comes out of it is.

What I think differentiates books from literature is that the book is about what the book is about.  The plot. If it's a murder or a spy or whatever, that's what it's about. Whereas for The Brothers Karamazov the plot is just a vehicle to explore ideas.   

For me the difference between normal movies and art movies is similar.   An action  movie just has to look cool, and probably won't challenge me with themes.  Even when it tries, it'll probably badly done, like The Matrix being passed off as much deeper than it was.  Or like Ii'm supposed t admire John Wick.  But for a film I usually see themes that challenge me, even make me uncomfortable.  For films, for me, it's about the feelings and aesthetics.  I may not even understand the plot.  In some films I'm not even sure how much of the stuff on the screen really happened, like Beau is Very Afraid.  But for me it's also not really the point.
That’s all fair! And I’m glad we could arrive at a solid middle ground. Doesn’t happen enough on social media lol.

i don't know, but whatever george stevens did with SHANE, to me - that's pure art. in shane, he treated the western genre with utmost admiration, respect and humility. no other ways to describe it, i simply think of shane whenever i think of movies as an art form.

the modern equivalent would be paul thomas anderson's the master, but it has too many nasty things in it, therefore i'm on the verge here: farting, hideous naked people, handjob, sex obsession etc. but other than that, yes, the master is the closest modern movie that is art to me.

notable modern contenders: silence, inside llewyn davis, the passion of the christ, the wrestler, nightcrawler, there will be blood, under the skin

I have a hard time considering any comic book film high art because you know before you walk in who is going to win. Plus the source material. I find comic book films boring as an adult because once you know the hero is always the winner, why even bother? I get that special effects can be visually stunning. But I could just go to a museum to see beautiful images. Calling a comic book film high art is like calling Feivel Goes West high art.

I have heard of this sort of definition, basically the curation of pieces where even if you didn’t make it, you bring attention to the aesthetic experience of something. Where even a dadaist mass produced urinal now qualifies as art even as it was posed to criticize the concept of art in the time.

I would agree that both examples register as an aesthetic experience but can they be ranked or distinguished in any way? Is a pop song satisfying in the same way as some other piece? But what I do find compelling is your point of how popularity or being mainstream is no meaningful distinction and artworks do shift categories while they themselves do not change as a piece. 

But I do think if there is a distinction to be made it has to be in how art work is experienced and even if that is a shift it comes from a shift in how the work is experienced or considered. Shakespeare’s work may be for the general public but analysis of such works shows their complexity and depth that makes them compelling to this day, they maintain relevance.
The standing the test of time at least tends to be a market of great works because others are forgotten. Not that they can’t be rediscovered, but there is something valuable in works that are still widely regarded. 

I guess I can only think of the need for a distinction being the desire to carve out a niche and rank ones tastes as superior. Whether it be of a wealthy class over the common folk, or intellectuals marking themselves apart from others. It becomes arbitrary as its about social dynamics and demographics. We all think what we value is the best for everyone, we universalize our preferences often.
Your last paragraph makes me think of Pierre Bourdieu's ideas on the politics of taste and the concept of cultural capital.
Battleship Potemkin is sometimes considered to be both an exceptional work of cinema and propaganda.
